chunks: Ali ibn Muhammad, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Muhammad ibn al-Rayyan, who said:

I wrote to Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him): 'A man fulfills something from his fifty [outstanding] prayers in the Sacred Mosque, or in the Mosque of the Messenger (peace be upon him and his family), or in the Mosque of Kufa. Would the one rak'ah be reckoned for him with the multiplication of what has come from your forefathers (peace be upon them) regarding these mosques, to the extent that it would suffice him, when there are ten thousand rak'ahs upon him, if he were to pray one hundred rak'ahs, or less, or more? And what would be his state?'

So he (peace be upon him) signed: 'It would be reckoned for him with the double [reward]. But, if there happen to be shortened ones from the prayer, (these would be) at their state. So he would not do it except for the increase, being closer to it than the deficiency.'

key_terms.الصَّلَاةِ الْخَمْسِينَ: the fifty prayers (referring to a specific quantity of missed prayers)
key_terms.تَقْصِيراً: shortening or deficiency (in the count of prayers)
key_terms.قَضِي: to fulfill or make up (missed prayers)
key_terms.مَسْجِدِ الرَّسُولِ: the Mosque of the Messenger (in Medina)

ai.seo_question: Does praying missed prayers in holy mosques multiply the count of fulfilled prayers or just the reward?
ai.summary: In this reply from Imam al-Baqir (AS), the distinction is made between the quantitative fulfillment of the obligation (where one rak'ah counts as one) and the qualitative reward (which is multiplied). This clarifies that the spiritual merit of praying in the Haram or Masjid al-Nabi does not reduce the number of units required to make up a missed prayer, ensuring the duty is fully discharged while maximizing divine reward. This ruling underscores the Shia principle that location enhances reward but does not alter the structural requirements of the prayer itself.
